utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would just like to inform you of something briefly, but for that purpose we would need to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two witnesses, Witness 5 and 6, Puskar, Stankovic. For Puskar we have got four and a half lines of summary, for Stankovic, we have three lines of summary. We would ask once again, please, could we have appropriate summaries of reasonable duration dealing with the factual issues to which they are to give evidence. If that is not done, of course it is a matter for the Court. We will object to any factual matters that are not disclosed within the summaries if my learned friends wish to adduce that in chief. That is the only matter that I wish to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The two witnesses referenced by my learned friend Mr. Moore are peculiar witnesses for us. We only talked to Mr. Puskar once briefly. One of our investigators did, in fact. I expect that once he's here, we shall have an opportunity to have a lengthier interview with him, after which my learned friend will be duly informed and a proofing note will be submitted to him. My learned friend has referred to the summary, and I'm sure he has realised that the summary is about one central fact, which is detailed in that summary. As for Witness Stankovic, we got in touch with him before the start of the OTP case. After that we were here, whereas Mr. Stankovic is now the Defence Minister, which I believe Mr. Moore is aware of. He has many commitments. The Defence team is trying to get in touch with him, but we are still not certain whether on account of his commitments he will be able to appear. There is also the possibility that we shall have to drop him or seek an alternative. As for the subject matter of his evidence, I believe my learned friend is well aware of that, too, although if Mr. Stankovic does appear, we shall have a interview and produce a proofing note which shall be duly submitted to the Prosecution. He was the chief medical examiner in Vukovar performing most of the autopsies. He performed the autopsies on most of the bodies that found in Vukovar and its surroundings. At any rate, as soon as we have more from these witnesses, as soon as we have conducted lengthier interviews, the OTP will be duly informed, including the relevant proofing notes possibly containing more information than the summaries themselves contain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the position is less than satisfactory for the efficient conduct of this trial. The Chamber has no idea, apart from those few lines, what it is each of these witnesses is to deal with or what you would intend that the witness would deal with. Under the system which is in place under the rules, unless you have the leave of the Chamber you will be confined in material facts to the matters on which you've given notice. I gather from what you have said it's your expectation, at least, that I'm of these witnesses would give evidence about other matters, which has certainly not been the subject of summary and notice. In the case of Mr. Stankovic, one of the consequences of what is happening is that if he should come here and you wish to speak about -- him to speak about other matters and you're given leave, it could be that he would be required to come at a later time for cross-examination, which is hardly the way Mr. Stankovic, I'm sure, would hope that his evidence could be dealt with. He would, I expect, want to be here once and once only and for as short a time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Thank you very much, Your Honour. And you are entirely right. Mr. Stankovic is a pathologist. He's a forensic expert, and he will only address the issue of autopsies. He will not be addressing any other issues. He will be commenting on the autopsies that he performed in the Vukovar area and the bodies that he examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that we understand, but that is not an adequate summary of the facts about which he will give evidence. What is it that he wants to say about the autopsies? What are the results that are material to your case? They're the facts that need to be briefly identified in the summary. If you give attention to that and bear that in mind as you make the time for Mr. Stankovic's arrival, and also bear that in mind in the summaries for all witnesses you wish to call, because it is those summaries that enables the Trial Chamber to understand what is being called, and the Prosecution and the other two Defences to prepare to know what this is being to be talking about. So we need to get that functioning properly, and notice needs to be given before the witness comes so that all counsel and the Chamber can prepare. As you know, if there's some particular difficulty, this Chamber is prepared to be understanding and oblige other counsel to put up with short notice, but it's not fair to them or to the Chamber for -- to have this operating for all witnesses. It's got to be something special and unusual. Your normal practice has to be to get this in order, and also to get a clear future planning of the witnesses who are to be called in which order. It's no good finding that the witness who is number 18 on your list arrives tomorrow unless there has been adequate notice of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I deal with two other small matters now that we're dealing with administrative details? They will not take a long period of time. We know obviously that Coric is a witness today. I believe Minic is a witness either today and tomorrow, but we are not aware of exactly who the witnesses are after that. Perhaps my learned friend, perhaps it's just misunderstanding, perhaps that can be clarified over the break. As I say, I don't blame. It's perhaps just a misunderstanding. That is the first point. The second point relates to the case of Mr. Radic. In July, we sought waivers in relation to four witnesses. My learned friends were aware of that. I believe from memory, the 27th of July there was a reply by the Radic team that waivers had been applied for and there we left it. Our understanding is we should have had a mission going to Belgrade today. We have had to cancel that, the reason being from what we understand from Belgrade is that three of those waivers have not been granted and one still has not been applied for. I do not know if that is right or wrong, because there does seem to be an area of confusion between Belgrade and perhaps my learned friends, and I don't blame them in any way. But clearly if these witnesses are to be called, we would wish to interview them and speak to them. My learned friends are aware of that fact. And I would ask them if perhaps they could make their own inquiries and clarify exactly what has happened so that we can move expeditiously and no time will be wasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That second matter, Mr. Moore, we will leave for your discussion with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I would anticipate that the matter can be resolved between you. If not, no doubt we will hear more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first matter, what was that? Would you remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that Minic, if that's his name, will be the next witness after Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Simply order. Yes, that's right. I've already mentioned to Mr. Vasic that there is need for order to be clarified and that system of advanced notice of order being maintained by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure that that will resolve itself. We all appreciate that for unfortunate reasons the start to the leading of the evidence by the -- Mr. Vasic and Mr. Domazet has not been as smooth as it ought to be, and we all look forward to that being resolved in the course of this week so that the trial can proceed efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'd better have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card that's given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us your first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: My name is Velimir Milos Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can't hear the witness properly. May he please be asked to move closer to the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We seem to have some problems with the sound and the interpreters hearing you. Therefore, I would ask you to move closer to the microphone and repeat your name?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Velimir Milos Coric. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Given the fact we speak the same language, and my questions are being interpreted as they must be, as well as your answers, so that everybody can follow what we're talking about, please make a short pause after each of my questions before you embark on your answers, and please follow the cursor on the screen. When you see a sentence end, please start your answer, sir. Sir, can you please tell us about your educational background and your rank in the JNA, and which rank did you hold at the time of your retirement?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I had completed primary school, a gymnasium, and a teacher training college, which is the equivalent of secondary education. Then I went to the military academy for the land forces military academy, and after that I also attended and completed the higher military academy. I served in a number of different places, but I spent the most time in Sarajevo and Belgrade. My duties ranged from platoon commander to brigade commander. When I retired, I worked as an administrative clerk in the secretary under the federal -- in the secretariat under the federal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what was your rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What we are talking about here is in relation to 1991. I would like to ask you this, sir: Back in 1991, did you ever go to the Vukovar front? If so, how many times?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I was there once, the last time in 1991, in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say late that year. Do you remember the circumstances that brought you there? If you could please elaborate. When specifically in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Officially I arrived in Njemci -- or, rather, in Negoslavci, my mission being to tour the units following the liberation of Vukovar. I was also supposed to have a word with the units to see what the condition was of the men there as well as their equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you arrived in Negoslavci after the liberation of Vukovar. Can you please tell us how many days precisely, if you remember, how many days after the liberation of Vukovar your visit occurred?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I wasn't assigned a vehicle straight away on the very day of liberation. I was only assigned a vehicle two days later, and that was when I left for Vukovar with an official driver assigned to me in an official car pursuant to an order of the chef de cabinet of the federal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you left pursuant to an order of the chef de cabinet. Can you tell us which vehicle you used, and did you have anybody escorting you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have escort. Part of my trip was dangerous. You couldn't exactly just drive along as a tourist would have. I was escorted by warrant officer second class from the same command. We were using a combat vehicle -- a military vehicle with military insignia driven by a civilian driver serving in the JNA, a professional driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go on this official trip armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, the section of the road between Sid and Negoslavci was risky, dangerous in terms of how safe it was. Whenever a JNA officer leaves his barracks officially on business, they always carry weapons, normally a pistol. In addition to a pistol, myself, the driver, and the warrant officer also each had a long barrel on us, an automatic rifle, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember what time of day it was when you left for Negoslavci, when you left Belgrade for Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I came to work that day. That normally started at half past 8.00 in the morning. After that the driver reported to me, so he was good to go and he was waiting for me in the front yard of the General Staff building. It was about an hour later after we had first reported to work the three of us were off, the driver, myself, and the warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recall which route you took to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. The order said route, mission, and approximately the hour at which we had to complete the mission on that day. The route to be taken was Belgrade, along the motorway until the forking off to Sid, from Sid to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anybody intercept you on your way there or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Not just myself but at the point of exit from Sid there was a -- a checkpoint, a swing gate where all the vehicles would be pulled over, including mine. Since all the police officers knew me because we had frequently gone on target practice in Sid, as soon as I approached the checkpoint, the police officer there recognised me, greeted me, and I went past.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On your arrival in Negoslavci, what did you do next? Did you come in touch with anyone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the standard military practice, I have to report to the local commander, and so I did. I reported to Colonel Mrksic. Since I did not know the disposition of his units and I wanted to tour them, he assigned me with an escort, a major, who took me to see the units, and I saw the artillery battalion, that's to say, the light rocket artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you stay at Colonel Mrksic's for a while or not on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for that. He, on the other side, did not have time to talk to me, but we agreed on one important matter. He asked me when I was due back, and I told him that I would like to return early in the afternoon before the -- before dusk, and he asked me not to hurry on my way because he would like to come to Belgrade. And as far as security concerns, he told me not to worry about that, that he would see to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you at that point why he was heading to Belgrade or did your conversation end there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me at that point, but later on on our way back to Belgrade we talked in the car and he told me that he had an important meeting with the minister, the federal secretary at the General Staff. He told me that this was the reason why he came along with me, the reason also being that he would use this same vehicle, and that he would also seize this opportunity to visit his family and spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived in that sector with certain missions and that you told Colonel Mrksic that you had to tour some units, and he assigned you an officer for that purpose. Can you tell us which officer that was and which units -- units was it that you saw?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I wanted to see the logistical battalion and the light artillery battery. The officer assigned to me by Colonel Mrksic was Jovan Petrovic, who was available at the time, and Mrksic assigned him to escort me and see me through the area where his units were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In -- since this officer escorted you to this area, do you recall where the logistics unit that you saw was stationed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, let me first remind you of the following: I was the commander of the unit, so that I knew this particular major from before. The fact that he assisted me in touring these units was just the result of the goodwill exhibited by his commander and himself. I said that I wanted to tour these two points, that was the logistics battalion of which I didn't know before. And major took me to see the battalion that was stationed in the village of Brko [as interpreted]. I was particularly interested in the medical element of the logistics unit, to visit the wounded and to present them with modest gifts that I had taken along on behalf of the Federal Secretariat, which included juices that normally in peacetime the soldiers would receive as part of their rations, several packages of cigarettes and two packages of biscuits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wish to make a correction of the transcript. On page 14, line 5, the village mentioned was Berak. Were you received by the commanding officer of the medical unit of the logistics battalion? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Bratislav Jovanovic, an old acquaintance of mine also, because he used to be the chief of medical corps in the brigade earlier when I served there. He received me there and took me to see the rooms where the wounded were put up. Later on we went to see the commanding officers and the civilian personnel working for the logistics battalion. We had a talk. I told them what I knew of the situation in the country at the time. We discussed the current events. They put questions to me and as far as I was able to I tried to explain to them the situation in which we were at the time. I can't tell you how long this took because I was not really pressed that far for time. I only recall that we talked until the time came when the army personnel had to go for lunch, and I joined them and had lunch with they will. I can't tell you roughly when it was, but it was during my visit to the area where the logistics battalion was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after visiting the logistics battalion, did you go to see any other part of the Vukovar sector?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said a moment ago, I had this other place that I wanted to visit. After we had our lunch, together with the major and the driver, we went to see the light rocket artillery battalion where we were met by Lesanovic, who has in charge of the unit. He could not stay with us for long because he had another obligations at the headquarters, but I stayed there with his subordinates and soldiers where we also discussed the events of that day and of the previous day. Specifically, in addition to Lesanovic, I was also received by persons who were officers also at the time I served there but had in the meantime been promoted, captain Savo Cvetanovic and Mijatovic whose first name I can't recall but they were the same generation of officers. I said Savo Cvetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember -- did you find out where the unit was stationed? Did you see where it was stationed, in what part of town?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I was able to see where it was. There was a checkpoint at the gate to what was formerly a winery in Vukovar. The hosts met me there, and they told me that the unit was stationed within the compound of the winery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us if you remember what you did there and how long the visit to this unit lasted.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to see about the time. I had the approval from Colonel Mrksic that I need not move in haste. So that would be one time reference. The other time reference would be that I had to talk to people and inform them about the matters from my purview. Just as with the other unit, I went for lunch with them here. I spent the whole afternoon with the unit until it was time for supper, which normally takes place at 7.00 p.m. That was when the soldiers started preparing for line-up and for supper.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you join them for supper?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Not this time. I did not have the appetite. I wasn't hungry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: We were waiting for a call from Mrksic from the headquarters in order to proceed on to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this call take place and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: The call took place a bit before the army personnel started preparing for supper. I was told that I should report to the headquarters and that Mrksic would be there waiting for us. So it was that major and I set off for the headquarters. Petrovic got out of the car, Mrksic got in the car, and we proceeded along the following route: Negoslavci, Sid, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what time of day it was? And I mean the point when you set off along the route toward Sid.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: If you followed what I was saying, we left Negoslavci at around 7.00 p.m., because that was when normally the supper in the army would take place. Then we had to drive over to the headquarters, and we could have reached the headquarters by 7.30 or 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you told us that it was roughly 7.30 or 8.00 p.m., can you tell me whether this was already at night-time? Was it dusk or was it still daytime?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That bit I remember, because I said at the start of my evidence that I told Mrksic that I would not want to head back by night. At this point in time, it was -- it was dark because it was night-time already, and this was something that I expressed my fears about. However, Mrksic sought to that bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say Mrksic saw to that. Can you tell us in what way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: You know that the commander is entitled to an escort in peacetime and in time of war, be it within the area where his units or deployed or outside the area. He exercised this right, and we had his escort that followed behind us on an APC. At any rate, it was a military police vehicle that escorted us and drove behind us. It was a commander's escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic have personal security guards in the car when you were with him together on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: If we do not take into account the vehicle that drove behind us, then we can say that he did not have any, but there was no need for that because in the car there was the driver, the major [as interpreted], Mrksic and I.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Warrant officer, Mrksic and I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there was no need for that. There could have been another car but he decided that one car was enough. And besides, the driver, warrant officer and I were also armed, and we also in that sense amounted to a certain form of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I just want to intervene into the transcript. Page 17, line 23. The transcript reads "driver, the major, Mrksic and I." It should read, "the driver, the warrant officer, Mrksic and I." Sir, what about the military police vehicle? Did it follow you all the way to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need. It followed us as far as the swing gate at Sid where we were again stopped by the police officers manning the swing gate for a short check. Mrksic took the opportunity to leave the vehicle and dismissed the escort vehicle. We had been outside the combat area by now, and there were no longer any security reasons or any real danger for the remaining part of the way from Sid to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned twice already the swing gate or the checkpoint at Sid. Do you remember where exactly this checkpoint was? What was the environment like? I'm talking about the place where you were stopped. If you can remember, sir. If not, we can just press on.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: It's easy for anybody to remember. It was easy to notice and to remember. If you approach it from the direction of Negoslavci, the fact is we were stopped there. This was the -- the far end of the settlement. There used to be a market over there or something like that, but that was the only military detail or element along that entire road as far as Belgrade, the only such swing gate or checkpoint where we had to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How long did you stay in Sid for on that occasion at the swing gate?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. Very briefly. There wasn't anything much that needed doing. The policemen recognised us. They recognised Mrksic and recognised me. They asked us if we had anything in the trunk, and we said nothing at all. They said any weapons, and we showed them the weapons we were carrying. There was no problem, really, because they knew who we were, and they knew that we were ordered back. They just let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you stopped anywhere else before you reached Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. The way into Belgrade was guarded and monitored for civilian and military vehicles alike. There was a swing gate across the entire span of the motorway, the entire breadth of the motorway. There were the usual toll booths, this time reinforced by blocks of concrete, and all the trucks and civilian vehicles had to take the left lane, whereas the military vehicles took the right lane on the hard shoulder, as it were, near the fields, the meadows. There were the police men regulating traffic and sending vehicles to the left or to the right depending on whether the vehicles for civilian or military. We reached this other checkpoint. There was a brief check, but we never encountered any other policemen until we reached our final destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long did you take at this checkpoint, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I'm truly sorry, I can't pinpoint the time down to the last minute. Only a few minutes. A brief stop, a very brief stop. As soon as the policemen recognised us, the colonels, immediately their behaviour was in line with that. They knew there was nothing that needed checking. They knew the vehicle was roadworthy. They knew we were officers, not to be thoroughly checked simply because there was no reason to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get from Negoslavci across Sid to Belgrade that evening when you drove with Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I know what the distance is, and I can try to think back. We had our dinner with the other soldiers first and drove from the battalion back to the command. If you take that into account, I would say that we left sometime between 7.30 and 8.00 that evening. And we could have taken up to one and a half hours to reach Belgrade. When I was back in the barracks, the reference point I used was I realised it was late at night already. But the thing is, I didn't really need to watch the time, nor was I told by anyone to watch the time and mind the -- the entire time line. It was, after all, a long time ago, and I'm not getting any younger myself. Therefore, I might be slightly wrong about the timing of this entire situation. Don't hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you left Negoslavci at about 7.30 or 8.00 that evening. You drove on for about one and a half hours. You arrived late at night. But if I add the whole thing up, it would seem that you arrive at about 9.00, 9.30 that evening, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking. I think your calculation makes sense. That's the way it was. When we arrived and I returned to my barracks, I realised it was late at night. It was before midnight, but it certainly was not early evening. And it's just as you have suggested. It may have been about 9.30 or 10.00 that we reached our final destination, Mrksic's flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you first drive to Mrksic's flat or did you first drive to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: It was late. We had no business over at the command, the headquarters. We drove straight to Mrksic's flat, because that was the only way for Mrksic to get there, the only vehicle he had, the one that we had arrived in from Negoslavci. So we took advantage of that and drove into his flat, after which the driver and myself returned to our own jobs, get a change of clothes, and we both drove back home once our mission had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you required to contact anybody at the federal ministry for All People's Defence once back from the mission or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Indeed we were. The cabinet itself did not comprise too many officers, mostly high-ranking ones, colonels and upwards. There were shifts of duty all the time, and whoever was on duty was authorised to give certain types of orders to authorise the use of vehicles, to receive reports from units on the ground and those of us arriving from the front. This duty officer would then submit this to the chef de cabinet. Colonel Nedjo Copic was on duty that evening. I told him that we were now back in Belgrade and that I drove Colonel Mrksic to Belgrade. I told him he came with us. But he was the very person preparing that briefing, and he knew that Mrksic was due for a briefing or a meeting with the federal secretary, didn't need telling. I went straight to my office and the warrant officer went straight to his own. I had a change of clothes. I put on my civilian clothes that I had worn to work that morning and I got into my car and drove back to my flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the meeting at the federal secretary, the date for that meeting was the 21st of November. In relation to that, can you determine the date that you were in Negoslavci and that you drove Colonel Mrksic back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: You mean a weekday or the date as in which date it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Day of the month, I mean.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's all right. As we were leaving Belgrade, I requested a vehicle on the day of Vukovar's liberation, but I wasn't authorised a vehicle the same day. I wasn't authorised one until two days later. Vukovar had been liberated on the 18th. So I got my vehicle that I'd requested on the 20th. It was on the 20th of November that I eventually arrived in Negoslavci. So all of what I've told you so far took place on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Coric. I have no further questions for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just try and clarify one or two reference points. You said that you went to Negoslavci and what I'd call the general Vukovar area on the 20th of November. I think that is correct, is not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Indeed. That's correct. The 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And during that day you had various appointments and meetings with individuals, some of which you remember reasonably precisely. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's correct. As I've pointed out already, me and those people go back some way, years back. It wasn't on that day that I met most of them. First of all, I was happy to see them doing well, alive and well. I was happy to meet them there. So this is an experience the likes of which can only be gone through by someone whose associates were as great as mine were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And would it be right to say that you remember the lunch with the officers and supper with the soldiers? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That is not right. I did not have dinner there. I did have lunch, not with the officers though. I had military rations together with the soldiers there, the foot soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sir, when you said that, "We had our dinners with the soldiers," you're not meaning to suggest the dinner at 7.00 in the evening? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I think the witness never said he had dinner with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vasic, he said he had -- firstly, that he didn't, and then later, when calculating times, he said that he did. So the matter needs to be clarified. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've heard the learned Judge's reply. When you say that you had dinner with the soldiers, was that with the soldiers there on the ground or with what I will call some of the soldiers or officers who were travelling with you? Can you clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I was crystal clear. I said 1900 hours, military dinner, military preparations for dinner. I used that as a reference point to calculate the time from there on. That's why I mentioned the military dinner. The soldiers were preparing to take dinner, but not me. I merely used that as a reference point, but I did not include myself, and I think I was perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, you were aware of dinner being taken that evening, military time, 7.00 thereafter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: To be quite precise, it was at 1900 hours or 7.00 in the afternoon. You can't have dinner at 7.00, can you? Again, I use this time as a mere reference point to know when I got there and when I left there, when I left the position of the light artillery rocket battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you read English? Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So looking at the screen, is it in English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just deal then with what you've said. Do you accept that you saw people having dinner at 1900 hours? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say they were having dinner. There is something in the army called preparation. They wash their hands, they prepare the rations, orders are read, soldiers are lined up. It is only after that that military dinner is taken. I didn't say I took dinner myself. I said they were about to. They were preparing. And I used that as a reference point to determine the time that evening to see if it was early or late, and then I arrived at the conclusion that the time might have been at about 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you as a civilian to tell me whether in actual fact there is a set time for the serving of dinner within the JNA army in 1991. That's all I'm asking, just information.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner always take place at a time that is strictly determined. You can have different kinds of food, dry or cooked, but always at the same time ordered by the commander. There is always an order determining the exact time at which breakfast, lunch, and dinner are to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I'm simply asking for information. What was happening at 1900 hours in the kitchens or whether they were going to be served. Can you just tell us, are they preparing? Are they serving? Are they lining up? I'd like to know, please, in more detail what you're saying is happening at around about 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I've told you, haven't I. I wasn't in the kitchen myself. I did not take dinner. All I said was the soldiers were preparing for dinner. When I say "preparing," every soldier knows what that means and when dinner is taken and when dinner is served.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer is you really don't know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I've asked you about four times, can you give us the actual -- what people are doing at that time? Are they preparing food? Are they serving food? Are they washing their hands? Because you seem to be very precise about it. And I want to know why you were so precise. What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: They were carrying out preparations for dinner at 1900 hours, sir. After preparations, there's the line-up, there's the distribution of dinner. It's the military custom. I used to do that myself years ago. The schedule is ordered and very detailed. You know exactly when to do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of the people, who were queueing up for food, as a former commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No. I did not even go where the soldiers were being lined up. I was sitting with those officers in one of the rooms and we were talking. I couldn't see whether dinner was actually being served, nor did I have any reason to go and check. There was nothing I could do about it. I couldn't help it, and I could do nothing about it. I simply mentioned that as a reference point for the time, I left the winery sector and was off to the brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us in your evidence that you think that you left somewhere between 7.30 and 8.00. And secondly, you believe the journey took about one and a half hours. That's what you've told us in evidence. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's right. I did say that. I can only confirm that. That's why I mentioned 1930 hours as some sort of a reference point, reference point in time for us to proceed on the basis of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Later on you actually said when you arrived in Belgrade that it was not early evening. You then said it may have been 9.30 to 10.00 p.m. Do you remember saying that? Because you did.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then you also said, "It was before midnight." Now, I want to deal with that particular phrase, "It was before midnight." Would it be fair to say that if you're talking about accuracy here that you are satisfied that it was before midnight, but your estimate is somewhere between 9.30 and 10.00? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I said before midnight, that was because we were there before midnight. We all know what midnight means. It could have been by midnight. But I also said that dusk was long gone by the time we got there. We had already reached halfway between Sid and Belgrade by the time dusk fell, and when we arrived it might have been 9.30 or 10.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with the distance? From memory I seem to remember it is about 130 or 140 kilometres between Negoslavci and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: A figure that rattles in my head is 157. Does that rattle anything in your head at all?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: 160, roughly speaking. I think you could round it off to your figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just work on the 160, if I may. Armoured personnel carriers, from having unfortunately dealt with armoured personnel carriers, they tend to move rather slowly on occasion. Do you agree with that, compared with an ordinary private vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's right. But even civilian vehicles did not drive at full throttle exactly. We knew we were being followed by a combat vehicle that could only go as fast as 50 or 60 kilometres per hour. We stuck to that sort of speed. Our own passenger vehicle drove at that speed, and so did the combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you about this combat vehicle? Armoured personnel carriers tend to come in three forms from memory. One is it is only tyres, one it is tyres and half track, and third is full track. What was the armoured personnel carrier that was following your vehicle that evening? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: The Combat vehicle was behind us. I couldn't see its tyres or its caterpillars. It was driving behind us at a distance of perhaps 50 or 60 metres. I was not able to identify the vehicle exactly but I know the vehicles we have. They usually have wheels and sometimes they are as fast as passenger vehicles or thereabouts. So there you have it. We were probably being followed by a vehicle powerful enough to keep abreast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In relation to distance from Negoslavci to Sid, again I require your assistance on that. What would that be, about 50 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I think even less, but I never kept track of that. There was never any need for me to. But we might as well get a map and have a look if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and ensure we'll get one. We're about to end this section, I believe. Can we deal with it this way: There was always concern on the Negoslavci to Sid road that there might have been some form of military incident? Would that be correct? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. Incidents did happen. They weren't that frequent, but some did happen. There was no incident on our way there, and we just reached our destination in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When one is travelling at night in military vehicle or military convoy, there are various ways of doing it. One can put the lights on, or one can use dimmed lights, and sometimes if the moonlight is bright enough, you don't use any lights to attract the attention of snipers. Would you agree were that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Snipers couldn't harm us at night. As for the rest, you're quite right. If there's a convoy, lights are dimmed. We call those dimmed lights military lights. But this was not a war zone, and we behaved just as ordinary passengers would have. Between Negoslavci and Sid was a different story altogether, but from Sid to Belgrade we were just passengers in a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the route from Negoslavci to Sid. Firstly, I would submit -- sorry, wrong forum. I would suggest that you drove more cautiously on that stretch of the road. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by more cautiously. The driver is a professional who has long-standing experience in driving, because he hasn't started driving at that point, and he does his job well. And I myself did not pay attention to him. Had there been an incident, I would have been aware of it. In the army, of course we always take measures to avert any incidents. In this case we did that, and there was no need for any special security arrangements other than the ones we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm suggesting to you is this: On the trip from Negoslavci to Sid, you travelled more cautiously. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because this was the dangerous area, and of course we were more cautious on that stretch of the road than afterwards. But this does not mean to say that we drove at a slower pace, rather, that our level of alert was higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, if it's 160 kilometres, bearing in mind you go through 50 kilometres, if it be that, of difficult terrain and a hundred kilometres towards Belgrade, would you assess that that journey would have taken somewhere between two and a half and three hours? Would that be a fair estimate? And that is why you think it was before midnight.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: As far as the distance is concerned, I already said that I wasn't sure about the exact number of kilometres. However, the stretch of road between Sid and Belgrade could be covered more quickly than the earlier stretch. At some sections of the road the driver may even have speeded, although I had confidence himself because he was a professional driver. In some cases the stretch of the road can be covered in less than hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But all I'm suggesting is if you look at the two things, one, that you feel certain that you got back before midnight; and two, given the road difficulties between Negoslavci and Sid but not road difficulties between Sid and Belgrade, the time estimate of between two and a half to three hours would be fair.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Two hours would be fair, in my view. As I said, the stretch of the motorway between Sid and Belgrade can be covered in about 40 minutes if you drive at 140 to 150 kilometres per hour. So my estimate would be closer to two hours than to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not going to go into the minutiae of that. Let us deal with one or two other areas. Clearly you had as you knew him, Colonel Mrksic in your vehicle. As you say. You have been to Vukovar and you have seen the general well-being of some of the troops. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I apologise. You have got Colonel Mrksic in the vehicle. He is of equal rank to you. Sometimes junior officers don't like to speak to senior officers and vice versa, but both of you are of the same rank, basically. That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's right. The two of us were of the same rank, but we were also comrades, and not from the day before but back from mid-1970s. Whenever we are in front of soldiers and when the soldiers are lined up, we know how to behave. However, privately we are comrades, and we do not pay attention to ranks or duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But actually, you're more than a comrade, are you? You're actually a good friend of Mr. Mrksic. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I've known Mrksic when he was a young man, when he came to the brigade. Then he was -- to the Guards Brigade. Then he was assigned to other units and then was again assigned to my unit where he was the Chief of Staff, and you can't get closer than that. In addition to the military duties that we had, we developed a relationship, a friendship of comradery which did not pay any particular attention to the ranks that each of us held. We were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's actually more than that, isn't it, within a guards regiment, because it is the elite regiment, officers tend to be very protective of one another. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise. I don't understand which way we protect and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's set aside malfeasance for a moment. Let us set aside bad dealings. We'll just deal with general dealings. Would you accept in a guards regiment because its elite nature that the officers tend to support one another as and when they can?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: To support a different matter. In the times of war we lent support to each other especially where one person is wounded and the other isn't. We even risk our lives. In peacetime we support one another as members of the Guards Brigade. In our opinion, the relations between officers have to be human. The situation may be different compared to some armies in the West. You're right that the colonel can't go along with the lieutenant colonel and so on and so forth. The superior/subordinate relationship is difficult. However, in our case, we called ourself the Yugoslavia People's Army and the situation was quite different. One has respect for the other person regardless of the rank the person holds and the line of profession the person comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I've nearly finished with this topic, but it might be an appropriate moment just to deal with the break now if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is just the right time, Mr. Moore. We will have the first break, resuming at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, when you arrived in Vukovar, did you actually go to the Vukovar Hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No, and I don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were travelling in the car on the way back to Belgrade, I presume that you had some discussions with Mr. Mrksic. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We talked, but we did not select specific topics or think of the conversation in advance. It was just a chitchat as we'd call it, without any particular order or any specific subject matter. We inquired after each other's families and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was he concerned about anything at all?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You have to ask him. This wasn't something I was able to notice. First of all, I wasn't interested, and second of all, it was night-time. I couldn't really see his facial expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can't ask him because he doesn't want to come out to play, as is his right. So I'm asking you. So what were the topics that you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I told you, sir, that I can neither remember nor were these topics taken in any particular order. You know how it is when you chat with someone. You don't touch upon anything specific. I knew why he came along with me, because this was something he told me at the outset, at the start of my journey, but we did not discuss about anything else. There was no need for that. And besides, we were not alone in the car. So it boiled down to chatting. All four of us took part in the conversation, Colonel Mrksic, the warrant officer's driver and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So in reality, you are remembering this trip 15 years ago from memory; is that right? There is nothing else to refresh your memory, no document, no reference document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: The document pursuant to which I travelled and pursuant to which I was supposed to come to Negoslavci must exist, although I don't know where it is. I recall that I was able to be assigned a car, a driver, and I must have had papers underpinning my trip to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just say, I, in no way, am taking issue of whether in actual fact you went to Vukovar. What I am taking issue with is that Colonel Mrksic travelled with you back to Belgrade. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you why if you don't understand the question. Because Colonel Mrksic has on two occasions before courts indicated that he travelled in the morning. One of those times he said he travelled by helicopter. Would that surprise you, that he was going to Belgrade on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. The topic that my learned friend Moore is currently dealing with has I believe been the subject of evidence toward the end of the Prosecution case. At the time, it was said that such a case would be put only to one of the three if -- accused if they decided to testify. The statement that are referred to here which were given before judicial authorities in Belgrade at the time when he did not have a Defence counsel to represent him is something that should -- should not be referred in this case because I don't believe it is in accordance with the Rules or the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I don't understand those last comments, but I do understand, I believe, that you say that there was some undertaking or statement by the Prosecution about the use that could be made of these matters. That's your first point, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will clarify in two sentences. My learned friend referred to a statement made by the accused Mrksic while addressing the witness here. The only such statement by Mrksic could be the one that he gave to judicial bodies. I don't think that my learned friend can refer to such a statement and put it to the witness, because before this Tribunal we cannot put to witnesses statements given in other cases on the same topic if they did not have a Defence counsel at the time. I believe that this has already been a matter of discussion before the end of the Prosecution case. We have even filed a motion, and that was a motion filed by all the three Defence teams on this subject. The Prosecutor is here trying to use portions of the statement and wants to put them to the witness. As this is an outstanding motion, I don't think my learned friend should be using these earlier statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I'm not aware of any motion from -- during the Prosecution case that is still current, that hasn't been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, this is a very new one. Yes. Very well. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Three things. Firstly, from recollection, we had submitted that they should be permitted for cross-examination. Secondly, this witness gives evidence that is highly relevant to an issue for the Court to determine. Clearly, the issue is notice and goes to the very heart of the matter. This witness has said that Mr. Mrksic travelled with him. In our submission, this witness and the Prosecution should be entitled to put to this witness, to say quite simply what Mrksic has said and to see what this witness's reply will be. It might well be that he says "He is entirely wrong, my memory is correct," or he might say, for example, "I might be wrong. It might be a different day." Therefore, in our submission, the Court would be entitled to assess the reply of the witness on a salient point in relation to this issue. Thirdly, it is hearsay. I accept that, but hearsay is admissible. Those would be my submissions in respect of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In what respect is this hearsay? Could you remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Technically it is not hearsay as such because hearsay does not apply, and clearly it is in the hearing of the defendant. But I suppose if one was to submit in relation to it, it is a statement made by another person not in the presence of the defendant, but here of course it is the defendant, and therefore it doesn't apply. Really, I think the core issue of a person being reminded of a statement made by another person when this witness was not present. Perhaps hearsay is an inappropriate word for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand what you want to put to the witness are statements that you assert have been made by the accused himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- in other proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Dealing with this issue specifically. And it's not a case of extraction. It is a case of dealing with the issue that this witness has brought before the Court and the Court seeks, and the Defence of Mrksic seek to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this the subject of the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything further, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I would like to remind my learned friend of the fact that it was on the 12th of June, 2006, on page 10291, lines 24 and 25, when he asked of the Trial Chamber leave to put questions only -- to put questions concerning the accused about the -- what they had stated in statements before other courts of law. However, therein, he did not request that he be allowed to put such statements to witnesses. In addition to that, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order, the Defence responded to this motion, and my learned friend Moore should reply to that within eight days. I don't think it's appropriate of him to try and put portions of these statements to this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just deal with one -- two matters that my learned friend has raised. The first is we had no notice at all that this witness was being called or that in actual fact witnesses dealing with this topic were within the compass of the Defence case. We did not know that there would be what I would call a quasi-alibi. What was being suggested by the Prosecution was that Mrksic had gone by helicopter. The challenges that had been put were slightly unusual. They were not always constant. So that is the first thing. It is a slightly different issue. We were not placed on the notice that we are now on. The second is this. We only received a motion from the Defence, I think, on Thursday and we have seven days to reply and we are doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber, Mr. Vasic, will allow the questioning to continue but allow it subject to the Chamber's consideration of the written motion that has been put by Defence counsel, and actually allowing this questioning now is not in any way to predetermine or pre-judge our ruling on that motion, and it may be that all of this evidence will come to be excluded once we've considered the motion in detail. It may not. I don't know. But while the witness is here, in case the motion should be dismissed, we think the evidence should be recorded, and we will then decide what, if any, use may be made of the evidence in the context of the motion. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic appeared before what I will call courts on the 25th of February, 1998, and 17th of December, 1998, eight years ago, and he said to the court that he left at 8.15 in the morning. Now, he was actually saying the 19th, but without going into the details, he was a day out for various reasons. So he doesn't accept at all that he went by car with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On that statement, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On that statement, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Secondly, he gave evidence on the 17th of December, 1998, and there he said that he left at 0800 hours and he went by helicopter. Not by car, by helicopter, leaving in the morning. There's no reference whatsoever to him travelling by car. So I would suggest to you that your evidence is either mistaken or untrue. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this is for, but I can tell you that he did travel with me and that it was on the 20th. I don't know where you came up with the other information, but I don't know how you can take the liberty of offending me outright and telling me that I lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is not what I have said. The material that I rely upon has been taken in a court in Serbia on two occasions, with Serbian judges. Do you understand? It has got nothing to do with this Tribunal. It is to them that he has given that explanation. Do you follow me? I rely on that. What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present there when the statements were given before these courts. I can tell you what I told you before, that Mrksic travelled with me in the vehicle on the date that I mentioned. I cannot go into the other information that you may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well. Let me then ask you this: When was the first time that you were spoken to by lawyers acting on behalf of Mr. Mrksic in respect of this hearing?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Counsel Vasic spoke to me yesterday for the first and the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Whom have you spoken to in Belgrade prior to coming here in respect of the defence of Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I did not speak to anyone concerning the defence. I spoke to his associate concerning my travel arrangements. I'm not sure what his last name is. He phoned me and asked me when I could be ready for the trip, and that was the gist of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you then explain the following to me: I have got two summaries allegedly. The first relates to three lines, then there is an amendment giving us details of what you were going to say. Now, where did the Defence get this material from if you have only spoken to Mr. Vasic and his colleague about your travel arrangements?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What is your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just look to me for a moment? Look to your right. I have a document that is created by the Defence. We have your name. The first part has got three lines of what you are going to say. Without wishing to be discourteous in any way, it really says nothing. The second summary, however, is in darker print, you can see it, and it's probably 15 lines of what you are going to say when you came to give evidence. Now, I want to know where that material came from, because you said you only spoke to Mr. Vasic, that was yesterday, and this was served on the Court beforehand, before that date. So where did that come from?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the document is from. Can I take a look at it? Is this a statement of mine? Do you have my signature? I don't know. But I do claim that I didn't speak to anyone, and I don't know where you came up with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let me just give you a flavour of what it says. It gives your date and place of birth, 17th of the 7th, 1935. I won't go into where you were born. And then it goes as follows: "This witness was a commander of the Guard's Motorised Brigade before Mr. Mrksic took over that position." Well, clearly that can be found from anyone. "In the relevant period the witness worked at the cabinet of the secretary for national defence in Belgrade." Let's assume for a moment that can be obtained from someone. "On the 20th of November, 1991, this witness came to Vukovar using a military vehicle. He there met Colonel Mrksic, and they agreed that Colonel Mrksic will finish his duties on daily reporting with his subordinate officers and they will leave back to Belgrade with his car." Now, there is a statement of what you are going to tell us in very general terms. Are you saying that you have never told anyone what you were going to say until you saw Mrksic yesterday? Not Mrksic, Mr. Vasic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't share that with anyone, nor did anybody ever ask me to. The personal details that you've read out a minute ago, that's all correct. There are a variety of possible sources for that information. If you go through my files with the secretariat, you'll find that. So there's nothing there that isn't in the public domain. Where you get it from, now, that's a different kettle of fish, and it's not for me to ask I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to continue asking you. The following continues: "In the evening hours, they left Vukovar and arrived to Belgrade after hour and a half. They stopped in front of the building which was Colonel Mrksic's flat. Colonel Mrksic went home and the witness left." So "in the evening hours." That's not in the public domain, is it? So did you tell someone you were travelling in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Well, who could I have possibly told that and when, if I'm telling you I have never spoken to anyone with the exception of Mr. Vasic yesterday? Who could I have told? Who could have produced this? Who could have given it to you? That's what I'd be interested in finding out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what we'd be interested in finding out, how the Defence are producing documents before you actually give evidence and speak to Mr. Vasic telling what your evidence is going to be. Do you understand? This came in one or two weeks ago and was given to us by the Defence. Are you sure you haven't spoken to someone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Again, I've never spoken to anyone about that, nor was there any need for me to speak to anyone about that. The matters raised were do I wish to testify, do I wish to travel, and when exactly would I be ready, and that is what I spoke to his assistant about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I haven't quite finished. What about the hour and a half? Did you tell anybody before yesterday that the trip took an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: No. Yesterday, with you, a while ago, we just established that, didn't we, how long it would take from Negoslavci. And again, we didn't specify the mileage or the speed. It was all in the roughest possible terms. But nobody kept track at the time, so these are all approximations, the speed, the time it took, as well as the distance. I did not speak to anyone else about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't quite finish there either. "They stopped in front of the building in which Colonel Mrksic's flat is. Colonel Mrksic went home and the witness left." Where did that information come from? If in actual fact the first time you spoke to Mr. Vasic or his team was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Where I got this information or where someone else got this information? What is it you're asking me? I was myself outside Mrksic's flat. I drove him there, and that's why I know. How can anybody else possibly know? Well, how on earth should I know how someone else got hold of that information, how they wrote it down, and how they eventually got it through to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, it came to us from the Defence. Let us move on to one or two other topics that you may be able to help me with. What is the function of a Chief of Staff, please?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: The function of a Chief of Staff is such that all the ideas and assignments formulated by the commander in the headquarters are for him to give shape to, to draw the relevant maps. In peacetime he runs the training. He makes sure all the equipment is available. He is responsible and stands in for the commander in all things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that the function of a Chief of Staff is to be aware of everything that is going around around him and his commander? What I would call a second finger on the pulse.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: That is true in part, but he is a commander's deputy and assistant, but there are another five assistants who run their own sectors for which they are responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just listen, please, and see if you agree with this analysis, that the Chief of Staff directs the work of the staff. He is also the deputy commander of the brigade. The Chief of Staff in accordance with the commander's decisions has the right to assign tasks to subordinates. The staff consists of an operations and training organ, an intelligence organ, a recruitment and personnel organ, organs for combat arms and the office. Would you agree that that is a good description of the Chief of Staff's function?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: For the most part you have just encompassed most of his work, at least according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because I am reading from the brigade command, JNA brigade rules 116, paragraph 116, Exhibit 395. So if that is the brigade command and those are the rules, would it be right to say that the Chief of Staff is really the commander in a lesser form?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: You can't have two rules -- you cannot have two commanders according to the rules. You can only have one, the other being his deputy. So it's own logical for the Chief of Staff to -- to act as a deputy. The commander may indeed confer some of his powers on him and delegate responsibility in terms of giving orders and assignments, but the commander's word is always the last, and he is supposed to sign all the commands and all the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But when we deal with reality within a military hierarchy, it's also true to say, is it not, that the relationship between a commander and the Chief of Staff is almost a unique relationship. There is a close relationship between those two officers.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: The relationships are one thing, and real commitments and obligations are a different thing altogether, but the one thing applies to the commander, another to the Chief of Staff. They can work together. They can complement each other, but everyone has their own commitments and obligations within the headquarters or within the staff respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But wouldn't you accept from me that the Chief of Staff is one of those few officers who can actually go to a commander and discreetly question the commander's judgement on a topic? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I don't see why that should be done discreetly. The work is public by its very nature. Everything that goes on in a headquarters is a public matter. There is no need for any whispering, for any muttering under one's breath, especially when the staff are all together and working on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal, please, with the functioning of the security organ within a brigade? Would it be fair to say that a security organ itself -- I will use the phrase, my own phrase -- that a security organ to some extent is a unit that watches to see what is happening and assists if it becomes necessary?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of one thing. I would like to ask you one thing, both you and the Chamber. We are straying from the subject matter of my evidence here. We are talking now about the functioning of the staff and the command. We're talking about rules that I had left in my drawer along time ago and may have forgotten bits of them, if you allow. What do I think about the security organ? What do I think about its work? I don't know. When I retired or stopped doing that job 15 years ago, that was that. What do I think about all these things. I don't quite understand your question. Therefore, I cannot provide an appropriate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the topic's being foisted on the witness, by my learned friend Mr. Moore, are outside the scope of the examination-in-chief and they certainly do not go to the witness's credibility. Therefore, I don't think all these matters should be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, cross-examination is not confined to the subject matter of the witness's evidence in chief and credibility. Cross-examination can be at large as long as it is relevant and within the competence of the witness. In view of the witness's rank and experience, these questions are obviously within his potential knowledge. So the questions are proper. Whether the witness is able to remember and answer them is another matter. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is because you left the army -- when, please?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so as a result of leaving the army in 1992, it's difficult to remember exactly the functions of the security organ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Not that it's necessarily difficult, but I don't see the point. Why are you asking me to think back to those times and to think about the remit of the security organ? Should I speak about my own unit or organ? Should I speak about everything that you're suggesting? It's just that I fail to see the point or any purpose to it for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can you answer the following then: Is the function or was the function of the security organ to look for problems and prevent those problems if they arose? Would that be one of its functions?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure which problems you have in mine. You tell me the problems. Once you've made it clear, we can have a look. See if it's down to him, see if that's down to the commander, see if it's down to somebody different altogether. What is this problem that he should be preventing and not anybody else within the command or headquarters for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you say was the function of the security organ in 1991? You tell us what you believe its task, its function is.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR CORIC
